name: wc
one_line: print newline, word and byte counts for each file
plain: `wc` (word count) counts lines, words and bytes in a file or in text you pipe into it. It answers 'how many?'
In a pipeline, wc -l is the standard way to count results: how many matches, how many users, how many files.
when: Count matches: grep pattern file | wc -l.
Check the size of a file in bytes, or its line count.
Find the longest line in a file.

examples.title: Lines, words, bytes
examples.explain: Prints three numbers and the file name: lines, words and bytes.

examples.title: Just the lines  (-l)
examples.explain: Counts the number of lines. This is the one you use most.

examples.title: Count matches
examples.cmd: grep -c ' 401 ' access.log   # or:   grep ' 401 ' access.log | wc -l
examples.explain: grep -c counts directly; piping into wc -l works with any command, for example ls | wc -l counts files.

examples.title: Bytes and characters  (-c, -m)
examples.explain: -c counts bytes and -m counts characters. They differ for text with multi-byte letters such as é.

examples.title: Longest line  (-L)
examples.explain: Prints the length of the longest line. A very long line in a data file often means encoded or minified content.

examples.title: Several files and a total
examples.explain: With more than one file wc adds a total line (use --total=never to hide it).

options.plain: Print the number of lines (newline characters).
Print the number of words (runs of non-space characters).
Print the number of characters (differs from bytes for UTF-8).
Print the length of the longest line.
Read the list of file names from F, separated by NUL bytes (- for standard input).
options.use: Counting a huge list of files: find ... -print0 | wc --files0-from=-.

options.plain: When to print the total line: auto, always, only or never.

mistakes: wc -l counts newline characters: a last line without a newline is not counted.
wc file prints the file name too; use wc -l < file to get only the number.
Counting words in code or logs with wc -w is rarely meaningful.
try: Count the unique IPs in access.log using sort -u and wc -l.
Count the files in a folder with ls | wc -l.
Find the longest line of a wordlist.
see_also: grep(1) -c, awk(1) (END {print NR}), sort(1), uniq(1), du(1), stat(1).
